strengths: The problem class is important and hard to solve for traditional methods.
POMDPs are known to be hard to learn.
The proposed idea is interesting and the results are satisfactory.
The backtracking step seems the most interesting part.
The paper addresses a pertinent challenge by leveraging additional information to improve training in RL environments.
It is well-structured, clearly written, and easy to follow.
Empirical studies show consistent improvements over baseline approaches across multiple benchmark domains.
Effectively simplifies learning in a noisy or partially observable environment, compared to learning from scratch.
Thorough evaluation of the algorithm on many different kinds of environments, and good comparisons to other algorithms.
The guided policy search approach for POMDPs makes a lot of sense.
Proposition 1 is a nice insight, and helps to understand the fundamental soundness of the approach.
The empirical comparisons between the different proposed GPO variants and their analysis is extensive.
weaknesses: The proposed work largely overlaps with existing work [1], which is public since Feb 2024.
The method matches that of [1] where the teacher takes the state of the underlying MDP and performs policy mirror descent, and the student performs imitation learning.
The teacher collects data through environmental interaction and the student performs offline imitation, exactly the same as described in this work.
The additional loss term L4 appears to be exactly the asymmetric loss in [1].
A later work [2] also proposed the same framework while utilizing PPO as backbone.
The real contribution of this work seems minimal; the PPO implementation appears to be only a computational trick for stable training.
The novelty may be limited to the backtracking step (setting \(\mu^k = \pi^k\)), and its significance is uncertain.
Due to the backtracking step, Proposition 1 and 2 seem to hold little value, assuming KL(\mu||\pi) can be minimized accurately enough.
The overall usage of notation is abusive and reflects confusion in the paper writing (e.g., eq 9 and 10, \(o_g\) and \(o_l\) appear out of place).

In the experiments, PPO+BC performs worse than PPO, and PPO-V (asymmetric PPO) performs comparably to the best, raising questions about what truly contributes to performance; missing experiments on GPO without backtracking.
Lack of comparison with a standard teacher‑student paradigm where a teacher is first trained then a student, which is crucial for evaluating practical value.
The application of imitation learning is unclear because there are no demonstrations, making it resemble model distillation rather than IL.

Several modifications and “tricks” (GPO‑style update, RL auxiliary loss for GPO‑penalty, additional clip and mask) lack adequate empirical or theoretical justification, and no ablation studies are provided.
No comparisons with state‑of‑the‑art baselines, limiting ability to gauge relative effectiveness.
No discussion of related work.
Unclear usefulness of the algorithm; if a perfect simulation exists, a simpler map learning approach could be optimal, questioning the need for simultaneous full and partial observations.
The claim “without requiring RL training for the learner” is contradicted by introducing an RL objective; needs comparison with a straight learner on unaugmented noisy observations.
The proof of Proposition 1 in the Appendix should be referenced in the main text.
The general idea of GPS for POMDP is not new and has been proposed in [1]; the paper lacks appropriate reference and discussion.
Dismissing methods that first train a teacher then a student as “inefficient” is unconvincing without proper evaluation.
Empirical comparison misses SOTA baselines that first train a teacher (e.g., TGRL) and uses ADVISOR incorrectly by co‑training teacher and student.
Evaluations are on domains different from prior work; need comparison with previously published results to assess hyper‑parameter sensitivity.
Some claims need to be made more formal.
The paper should include a more in‑depth literature survey of GPS for POMDPs (e.g., work in [1] and its extensions).
Need comparisons to the original ADVISOR and PPO+BC where the teacher policy is first trained to convergence; TGRL significantly outperforms ADVISOR and should be added.
Lack of formalization of “hand‑wavy” paragraphs; claims about monotonic policy improvement and applicability to partially observable policies need formal statements.
Explanation that policy gradients for the learner suffer from high variance is vague and requires concrete statements; the intuition is not specific to the current method.
